title: Spring Rolls
subtitle: crispy fried rolls with pork and cabbage filling
excerpt: Golden, shatteringly crisp rolls filled with seasoned pork mince, cabbage and glass noodles, deep-fried at 180°C until blistered and crunchy. A Chinese New Year and dim sum classic. Makes 20 spring rolls.
sourceNotes: Spring rolls are one of the most internationally recognised Chinese foods. In China, the filled and fried version (chun juan) has roots in the spring festival tradition of eating long, thin foods to welcome the new season. They are documented in Chinese culinary texts from the Tang dynasty onward in various forms, with the fried version becoming prevalent in Jiangnan (Shanghai region) and Cantonese cuisine. The filling of pork and cabbage with glass noodles is a classic Shanghainese version.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the rolled, unfried spring rolls on a tray until solid, then transfer to bags. Fry from frozen at 170°C for 6 to 8 minutes until golden and cooked through.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The filling must be completely cold before wrapping. Make it a day ahead and refrigerate.

glossaryTerms.definition: Thin, square sheets of wheat flour dough used for spring rolls. They are sold frozen in Asian grocery shops and must be defrosted and kept covered while working to prevent them drying out. Thinner than wonton wrappers, they blister and crisp when deep-fried.

Literally 'breath of the wok'. The slightly smoky, charred aroma that develops when food is cooked over very high heat in a well-seasoned wok. Achieved at home by getting the wok as hot as possible before adding oil.
A Chinese rice wine with a nutty, amber flavour used widely in marinades, sauces and braises. Named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. Dry sherry is the closest substitute.
Finely milled maize starch used to thicken sauces and coat ingredients before frying. Mixed with water it forms a paste that seals spring roll wrappers securely before frying.

content.text: This recipe makes 20 spring rolls and takes about 60 minutes, including cooling time for the filling. The filling of pork, cabbage and glass noodles is cooked first, spread thin to cool, then wrapped tightly in
spring roll wrappers
sealed with
cornflour
paste and deep-fried at 180°C. A touch of
Shaoxing wine
in the filling adds depth;
wok hei
from high heat sets the flavour.
The filling must be completely cold and as dry as possible before rolling. Hot or wet filling makes the wrappers steam from inside rather than fry, and they will not crisp.
What you need

items.prepNote: mixed with 2 tbsp cold water to form a paste for sealing

soaked in hot water for 20 minutes, squeezed dry and finely sliced

content.text: Method
Heat 2 tbsp oil in a wok over high heat. Stir-fry the pork mince until browned, about 3 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, cook for 1 minute.
Add the cabbage and mushrooms and stir-fry for 2 minutes until the cabbage has wilted.
Add the Shaoxing wine, soy sauce, oyster sauce and glass noodles. Toss for 1 minute. Stir in the sesame oil.
Spread the filling on a wide tray and leave to cool completely, at least 30 minutes.

Place a wrapper on a clean surface in a diamond orientation. Put 2 tbsp of filling in the lower third. Fold the bottom corner up over the filling, fold in the sides, roll up tightly. Seal the top corner with cornflour paste. Repeat.
Heat the frying oil in a wok or deep pan to 180°C. Fry the spring rolls in batches of 4 to 5 for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve immediately with sweet chilli sauce or soy and rice vinegar for dipping.

items.symptom: Spring rolls burst open in the oil
items.cause: The seal was not firm, or the rolls were not tight enough.
items.fix: Roll tightly and press the seam with the cornflour paste firmly. Rest seam-side down before frying.

items.cause: Oil was not hot enough, or the filling was still damp.
items.fix: Make sure the oil reaches 180°C and the filling is completely cold and dry before wrapping.

items.cause: Too much filling or not rolled tightly.
items.fix: Use no more than 2 tbsp per roll and roll firmly, without gaps.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Fried spring rolls are eaten at Chinese New Year in eastern China to mark the start of spring. Fillings vary by region across China and Southeast Asia. The key is draining the filling well before rolling. Excess moisture makes the wrapper soggy and risks splitting during frying.
